anchor: The steel-engraved United States federal note and Treasury security — the guilloché lattice, the intaglio ink, the greenback green of the dollar, and the Treasury seal — read as the literal artifact of the thing this corpus is about: a 235-year fight over what American money is and who controls it.
rationale: Every chapter of this corpus is an argument about money itself — Hamilton's funded debt, Jackson's hard coin, the 1862 greenback (the first U.S. fiat note, a load-bearing claim in the history), Bretton Woods gold, the 1971 severing of dollar from metal, and the $39T of Treasury paper the system now rolls every month. The engraved federal note is the physical embodiment of that argument, so the corpus is dressed as one: the deep greenback green and near-black intaglio ink of currency, set on warm currency-paper cream, with a Treasury-seal bronze and a seal-oxblood as secondary inks. A high-contrast banknote Didone carries the display lettering (the denomination type of a bill); a warm body serif and a ledger mono complete the engraver's-and-Treasury-ledger world. Wavy guilloché rules and a central seal lozenge ornament the breaks. It diverges hard from the ad-tech teal/cobalt siblings, the broadcast-magenta Test Card, and the cool-serif philosophy corpora — this one looks like a dollar bill under the loupe.
